sections.title: Taxonomy and general form
sections.text: Thanatephorus cucumeris (A. B. Frank) Donk is the historical name given to the sexual stage associated with Rhizoctonia solani J. G. Kühn. The taxonomic databases consulted currently treat T. cucumeris as a synonym of R. solani, the accepted name, rather than as a separate species. In plant pathology, R. solani refers in practice to a highly diverse set of isolates divided into anastomosis groups (AGs). The fungus is usually encountered as vegetative mycelium; it is not a cap-forming mushroom.

sections.title: Hyphae and sclerotia
sections.text: Young hyphae are pale or nearly colorless, becoming tan to light brown with age. They are septate, and their characteristic branches often arise near a right angle, with a slight constriction at the base and a septum close to the branch point. The fungus persists in soil and plant debris as mycelium and as sclerotia, compact, irregular, brown to nearly black survival structures. Their appearance and abundance vary with isolate and conditions.

sections.title: Ecology and plant disease
sections.text: Rhizoctonia solani is a soilborne pathogen with a broad host range, but anastomosis groups and isolates differ in host range and aggressiveness. Depending on the crop and isolate, it can cause damping-off, root or crown rots, stem cankers, tuber lesions, or foliar blights. Sclerotia and mycelium can survive in soil or crop debris; moisture, temperature, and plant condition influence symptoms. Symptoms alone are not sufficient to identify the species without plant-pathology examination.

sections.title: Rare sexual stage
sections.text: Under some humid conditions, some isolates produce the sexual stage: a thin, whitish hymenial layer spread over plant tissue near the soil surface, where basidia bearing basidiospores form. This layer can be delicate and easily removed. The stage is encountered far less often than mycelium and sclerotia; it does not form a cap, stalk, gills, or pores.

traits: Soilborne basidiomycete usually encountered as vegetative mycelium called Rhizoctonia solani; Thanatephorus cucumeris is the traditional name for its associated sexual stage
Septate hyphae, often branching near a right angle with a constriction at the branch base and a nearby septum
Young mycelium pale, becoming tan to light brown; compact, irregular, dark sclerotia can act as survival structures
A highly diverse set of isolates grouped by anastomosis group, with variable host ranges and aggressiveness
May cause damping-off, root or stem rots, cankers, and blights depending on host plant and isolate
Rare sexual stage: a thin, whitish effused layer bearing basidia and basidiospores; no mushroom-like anatomy
safetyNote: This is a plant-pathogenic fungus with no food use described in this entry. This reference alone cannot diagnose a plant disease.
